sources.title: National Center for Home Food Preservation
sources.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia
sources.supports: Describes itself as a source of current research-based recommendations for most methods of home food preservation, established with USDA (CSREES) funding; separate sections for canning, pickling, fermenting, freezing, drying, curing and smoking, and storing; points to the University of Georgia Cooperative Extension book So Easy To Preserve (6th edition, reviewed and updated 2020).
sources.notes: Upgrades the register placeholder of the same id. Home page only; no specific recipe or process is taken from it.

sources.title: General Information on Pickling
sources.publisher: National Center for Home Food Preservation (University of Georgia), adapted from USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, AIB 539 (rev. 2015)
sources.supports: Acidity in a pickled product is as important to safety as to taste and texture; do not alter vinegar, food or water proportions or use vinegar of unknown acidity; use only recipes with tested proportions; a minimum uniform acid level is needed to prevent growth of botulinum bacteria; in fermented sauerkraut and brined pickles salt is vital to safety and texture and must not be cut back; boiling-water canner processing prevents spoilage by microorganisms and enzymes.
sources.notes: Page states 'Reviewed February 2018' (day not given; 2018-02-01 is a placeholder day). The fermenting page (nchfp.uga.edu/how/ferment/general-information-on-fermenting/) carries the same text at the time of reading. No numbers, ratios or times from this page are reproduced in the archive.

sources.title: American cookery, or, The art of dressing viands, fish, poultry, and vegetables ... (Amelia Simmons, Hartford, 1796)
sources.publisher: Library of Congress, Rare Book and Special Collections Division (catalogue record)
sources.supports: Catalogue record of the digitized 1796 Hartford edition printed by Hudson & Goodwin for the author; title page lists vegetables, pastes, pies, preserves and cakes; cataloguer's note: first cook book written by an American and published in the United States; Library of Congress is not aware of any U.S. copyright or other restrictions on the digitized documents.
sources.notes: Only the catalogue record was read. The text of the pickling or preserving sections of the book was NOT read and no claim about its contents is made in the archive.

sources.title: About Botulism
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCEZID)
sources.supports: Botulism is rare but serious, caused by a toxin that attacks the nerves and causes difficulty breathing, muscle paralysis and death; five main kinds, all medical emergencies; common sources of foodborne botulism are homemade foods that have been improperly canned, preserved or fermented, and store-bought foods are uncommonly contaminated; see a doctor or go to an emergency room immediately with signs and symptoms.
sources.notes: Visible 'last reviewed' date on the page (April 18, 2024) precedes the 2026-02-26 update.

sources.title: Home-Canned Foods (Botulism)
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCEZID)
sources.supports: Follow safe canning instructions and use the right equipment; never taste food to see if it is safe; be mindful of the kind of food, jar size and packing method; the page lists home-canned tomatoes, low-acid home-canned foods and home-fermented foods among foods to boil before eating (times given on the page, not reproduced here); signs a container should be thrown out (leaking, bulging, swollen, damaged, spurting, discolored, moldy, smells bad); do not eat food if you do not know whether safe canning guidelines were followed.
sources.notes: The boiling times on this page are deliberately not reproduced in the archive.

sources.title: Canning and Food Preservation on the World War II Home Front
sources.publisher: U.S. National Park Service
sources.supports: Government, extension and commercial resources taught home preservation (drying, freezing, pickling, canning); sources discouraged canning vegetable mixes as too dangerous; root vegetables stored in cool, dark places like root cellars or in the ground over winter; canning was by far the most popular method; botulism possible if bacteria not eliminated; hot-water-bath for acidic foods and pressure canning for other vegetables and meats; more than 3,800 community canneries by the end of the war, with knowledgeable staff or volunteers ensuring safety; 75% of American homemakers put up 4.1 billion containers in 1943.
sources.notes: NPS heritage article, interpretive rather than a regulator. Page date not shown in the text read. Classed 'museum' as heritage interpretation.

sources.title: Home Storage of Fruits and Vegetables in Root Cellars (MP562)
sources.publisher: University of Missouri Extension
sources.supports: Quick-reference chart of temperature and relative humidity ranges by crop (cold and very moist for root crops and cabbage family; cold and moist for potatoes, apples, pears; cool and dry for onions, garlic, dry beans; warm for sweet potatoes, pumpkins and winter squash); do not store fruits with vegetables because ethylene shortens vegetable storage life; strong-smelling vegetables should be stored away from other food; do not allow fruits and vegetables to freeze; storage life depends on crop maturity, storage conditions and condition at storage time.
sources.notes: Page shows 'Reviewed January 2023' and 'September 2017' (months only; day set to the 1st). References listed on the page are 1979 and 1982 books.

sources.title: Oxon Hill Root Cellar
sources.publisher: U.S. National Park Service (Oxon Cove Park and Oxon Hill Farm)
sources.supports: Root cellar built in 1830 by the DeButts family, partially underground to keep its contents cool; before refrigeration, root cellars stored starchy vegetables that could last over the winter months without spoiling.
sources.notes: Short site description; no storage conditions or losses are given.

sources.title: Ice House
sources.publisher: Thomas Jefferson Foundation, Monticello
sources.supports: Jefferson designed an ice house, built by enslaved craftsmen under James Dinsmore, to store ice or snow for refrigerating fresh dairy and meats; ice harvested from the Rivanna River needed freezing weather and combined enslaved laborers and hired wagoners; Jefferson recorded 62 wagon loads to fill it at a cost of $70; Jefferson's note that at ice houses he saw in Italy about a third of the ice was lost by melting; ice lasted until October 15 in 1815; a 1810 record that the ice failed on September 14; in winter 1813 the ice house was filled with snow.
sources.notes: Encyclopedia entry quoting Jefferson's papers; the year of the 62-wagon-load fill is not stated in the text read.

sources.title: Refrigeration & Food Safety
sources.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.supports: Bacteria grow most rapidly between 40 and 140 degrees F (the 'Danger Zone'), some doubling in as little as 20 minutes; refrigerators should be set to 40 F or below; use an appliance thermometer; foods above 40 F for more than 2 hours should not be consumed.
sources.notes: Page last updated March 23, 2015.

sources.title: Cistern Safety and Disasters: Before, During, and After
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
sources.supports: Cisterns store treated public-system water or untreated catchment water (rain, ground, spring or surface); disasters can wash germs or chemicals into cisterns; water with fuel or toxic chemicals cannot be made safe by treating it; untreated catchment cisterns with open connections may fill with storm debris or floodwater, disinfecting them does not work well and the health department should be asked; use stored emergency water instead; post-disaster, use only clean treated water for drinking, cooking, ice, dishes, bathing, teeth and cleaning, while contaminated water may be used to flush toilets.
sources.notes: The page's cistern-disinfection dosing table is deliberately not reproduced in the archive (it covers treated public-system water in cisterns). Visible dates: published Sept 6 2024, updated April 1 2024, reviewed Aug 20 2024.

sources.title: Collecting Rainwater and Your Health: An Overview
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCEZID)
sources.supports: Rainwater is not necessarily safe to drink without first removing germs and chemicals; even clear rainwater can contain germs and chemicals; germs and chemicals (asbestos, lead, copper) can come from air, roofing, gutters, piping, storage materials and bird droppings; mixing rainwater with treated water can make the treated water less safe; use rainwater in ways that limit swallowing and prefer public-system or bottled water for drinking, cooking, teeth, rinsing produce; test regularly if drinking, cooking or bathing with it and ask the health department what to test for; first-flush diverters; screen or empty barrels at least every 10 days against mosquitoes; keep rainwater separate from piped water; collection is not allowed in all places.
sources.notes: Page lists no treatment recipe; it points to treatment methods and home treatment systems.

sources.title: Soak Up the Rain: Rain Barrels
sources.publisher: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (Region 1 / Soak Up the Rain)
sources.supports: Rain barrels capture roof water for uses such as lawns, gardens or indoor plants; cisterns are larger, above or below ground; roof runoff can pick up bacteria from birds and animals and chemicals from roof materials, factors to consider before using rain barrel water on edible plantings.
sources.notes: The page carries a disclaimer that it is no longer being updated and content may not be current, yet shows a 2026-10-20 modified date. It does not itself say 'do not drink'; the drinking caution in the archive comes from CDC.

sources.title: Cisterns
sources.publisher: Thomas Jefferson Foundation, Monticello
sources.supports: Jefferson had four brick cisterns installed from 1809 to collect rainwater from the roofs; two northern cisterns reserved for fire, two southern for kitchen, laundry and garden; he estimated they would supply 600 gallons a day; by 1815 he wrote that they would be useful only if he could make them hold water; in 1818 he called them useless for want of a proper cement; they were never completely watertight and only two reliably held water; Jefferson's own letter says he intended, to have potable water, to sink a sand-filled well beside a cistern, expecting water rising through the sand to be sufficiently purified, and had not been able to do it.
sources.notes: Encyclopedia entry quoting Jefferson's correspondence. Whether the sand well was ever built is not stated in the text read; the quoted letter says he had not done it 'as yet'.

sources.title: Water Supply (Fort Union National Monument)
sources.publisher: U.S. National Park Service
sources.supports: The fort's original source was Wolf Creek with water hauled by wagon; wells later (main well about 85 feet); in the mid-1880s indoor plumbing arrived; the fort kept a large supply of stored water for fire in cisterns filled by collecting rain water off roofs, each about 20,000 gallons, two at the hospital and two at the Depot; privies and large pits ('sinks') for waste disposal; a soldier's account of bathing in a borrowed tub; poor drainage and flooding at the second fort; ice cut from dammed creek ponds for the ice houses.
sources.notes: The page says the cisterns were for stored fire-fighting water, not for drinking. The text read does not describe the water quality in the cisterns.

sources.title: Inauguration of Restored Rain Harvesting Systems: San Juan National Historic Site
sources.publisher: U.S. National Park Service, San Juan National Historic Site (archived news release, 29 Nov 2011)
sources.supports: Spanish-built rain-harvesting cisterns beneath the plazas of El Morro (three cisterns, nearly a quarter-million gallons) and San Cristobal (four cisterns, over half a million gallons) were crucial to survival in the mid-1700s; religious images were painted on the walls for the protection of their water; after the 1898 Spanish-American War, U.S. Army personnel closed the cisterns believing the water had been poisoned by the defeated Spanish soldiers; restored in 2011 to supply non-potable water; potable supply planned as further work.
sources.notes: Archived NPS news release (content not updated since publication). Restored for non-potable use only, which the archive reports as the page states.

sources.title: About Water Disinfection with Chlorine and Chloramine
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCEZID)
sources.supports: In the United States, utilities first used chlorine to kill germs in tap water in 1908 and chloramine in 1929; utilities add chlorine or chloramine to tap water to kill germs; chlorine levels up to 4 mg/L are considered safe in drinking water; disinfection byproducts can cause health problems at high enough levels; utilities must meet water quality standards.
sources.notes: Visible Updated date (Feb 8 2024) precedes the Published date (Sept 16 2024); both recorded as shown.

sources.title: John Snow, Cholera, the Broad Street Pump; Waterborne Diseases Then and Now
sources.publisher: Theodore H. Tulchinsky, in Case Studies in Public Health (Elsevier, 2018), via PubMed Central
sources.supports: Snow's 1854 investigation of the Soho cholera outbreak; he traced cases to the Broad Street pump and the handle was removed; the epidemic was already declining as people left the area; Snow compared cholera deaths in houses supplied by two London water companies, one drawing from a sewage-contaminated part of the Thames and the other from upstream; during the first four weeks deaths in Southwark and Vauxhall customers were 14 times those in Lambeth customers.
sources.notes: The abstract says the removal of the handle 'led to cessation' of the epidemic; the body of the same chapter says the epidemic was 'already declining'. Both are recorded in the article.

sources.title: A map taken from a report by Dr. John Snow (Wellcome Collection, M4869)
sources.publisher: Wellcome Collection, London
sources.supports: Catalogue record of a map from Snow's pages 97-120 of the 'Report on the cholera outbreak in the Parish of St. James, Westminster, during the autumn of 1854', presented to the vestry by the Cholera Inquiry Committee, July 1855; the report covers cholera outbreaks in central London in 1832, 1848-9, 1851, 1852, 1853 and 1854, a public water pump in Broad Street, meteorological conditions, and population, housing, sanitation, sewerage, cess pools and the water supply of Soho; Public Domain Mark.
sources.notes: Only the catalogue record was read. No image is used in this archive.

sources.title: On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (John Snow), digitized copy
sources.publisher: Internet Archive (digitized copy of a Wellcome Library item, identifier b28985266)
sources.supports: Snow's own words on the 1854 Soho outbreak, as read in the machine-read text: that the pump handle was 'removed on the following day'; the observation that 'no brewer's men were registered' as dying of cholera; the description of the comparison of the water companies as an experiment 'on the grandest scale'; and a quoted statement by Arthur Hill Hassall that the water of the Southwark, Vauxhall and Lambeth companies is 'by far the worst' of those taking supply from the Thames.
sources.notes: Only short fragments were returned by the extraction; the whole 1855 book was not read. The edition and imprint were not read from a title page, so the archive calls it 'a digitized copy' and does not name an edition.

sources.title: Chelsea Waterworks Company: Purchase Records (GB 0074 ACC/2558/CH/05), biographical history
sources.publisher: AIM25 / London Metropolitan Archives (The London Archives)
sources.supports: Archive catalogue history of the Chelsea Waterworks Company: in 1809 it obtained powers to take water direct from the Thames, a source 'particularly polluted'; chief engineer James Simpson introduced slow sand filtration in 1829, a system still in use in 1974; following enforcement of the 1852 Metropolis Water Act the company opened a new intake and filter beds at Seething Wells, Surbiton, in 1856.
sources.notes: The collection itself is purchase records 1837-1876; the biographical history is the part relied on.

sources.title: Slow Sand Class: Part 1 of 4 (training slides, notes version)
sources.publisher: Oregon Health Authority, Drinking Water Services
sources.supports: James Simpson designed a slow sand filtration system for the Chelsea Water Company in 1829, the first use of slow sand filtration expressly to produce drinking water; the 1852 Metropolis Water Act required all water from the Thames within 5 miles of St Paul's Cathedral to be filtered; Snow recognised the value of filtration; the slides state that under proper operation and favorable raw water conditions slow sand filters can perform very well, with 2-4 log removals of Giardia and viruses and more than 4-log removal of Cryptosporidium; filters remove iron and manganese by precipitation, and cyanobacterial toxins are listed as a separate risk.
sources.notes: A state regulator's operator-training slide deck (77 slides) as returned by the extraction, not a peer-reviewed or guidance document; the training material is for water-system operators. Date 2024-03 is inferred from the file path (SSF-3-2024) and is approximate.

sources.title: 'A very interesting point in geography': The 1773 Phipps Expedition towards the North Pole
sources.publisher: Ann Savours (Mrs. Shirley), Arctic vol. 37 no. 4 (December 1984), pp. 402-450 (Arctic Institute of North America)
sources.supports: Scholarly account quoting the expedition record that Doctor Irving's apparatus for distilling fresh water from the sea produced water 'perfectly free from salt and wholesome, being used for boiling the ship's provisions', and that the quantity was generally from thirty-four to forty gallons 'without any great addition of fuel'.
sources.notes: The article is 27 pages; the extraction returned only the quoted sentences. We do not know from the text read what period the quoted quantity refers to, so the archive does not repeat it as a rate.

sources.title: Water purification prescribed in Ayurveda
sources.publisher: K P Skandhan et al., Ayu (journal) 2011;32(4):448, via PubMed Central
sources.supports: Reports that the Sushruta Samhita, an Ayurveda classic, describes purifying drinking water by keeping flowers (utpala, naga, champaka, patala) in it and decanting; the authors write that a standard measure for this is not known and that a scientific study on this aspect has not been done.
sources.notes: Only this passage was read. The article does not (in the text read) describe boiling, sand or charcoal; those claims about Sanskrit sources are NOT made in the archive.

sources.title: 'Cleanse or Die': British Naval Hygiene in the Age of Steam, 1840-1900
sources.publisher: Elise Juzda Smith, Medical History 2018;62(2):177-198, via PubMed Central
sources.supports: Royal Navy surgeons held that dryness, cleanliness and ventilation prevented disease; continuous washing and fumigating of decks; Norman Chevers's 1846 half-joking motto 'cleanse or die!'; from the late eighteenth century recommendations by Lind, Trotter and Blane led the Admiralty to reform sanitation, ventilation, diet, drink, clothing and bedding; the dominant explanation was noxious air (miasma), with a competing contagionist view; 'unwholesome effluvias' from spoilt cargo, bilge water and filth were blamed; it proved almost impossible to eradicate sickness at sea; the Admiralty's efforts raised health and comfort and produced a decline in casualties in the second half of the nineteenth century.
sources.notes: Read via an extraction of the article's opening sections (abstract, introduction and first section); later sections were not read.

sources.title: Edwin Chadwick: A Pioneer of Public Health Reform and His Role in Sanitary Awakening
sources.publisher: Pooja Mary Vaishali and Nisha Boopathy, Cureus 2024;16(9):e68858, via PubMed Central
sources.supports: Chadwick's 1842 'Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population' linked poor sanitation and disease; miasma theory held that diseases such as cholera were spread by foul air from decomposing organic matter, and encouraged efforts to clean up urban environments before germ theory was established; the report's proposed improvements were costly and the government of 1842 effectively rejected it until a Public Health Act in 1848 empowered local authorities to build sewers, provide clean water and regulate waste disposal.
sources.notes: A narrative review in a general open-access journal (Cureus); useful as a summary, weaker than specialist history. Not used for any contested claim.

sources.title: About Handwashing
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Clean Hands)
sources.supports: Handwashing with soap is one of the best ways to stay healthy and prevents the spread of respiratory and diarrheal infections; the five steps are wet, lather, scrub for at least 20 seconds, rinse, dry; if soap and water are not available use a hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol.
sources.notes: Visible Updated date (January 11, 2024) precedes the Published date (April 30, 2024); both recorded as shown.
